summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to run the ordering of materials for electrical work: building a bill of materials from the drawings, describing every item so that the right one arrives, timing orders against lead times and the job programme, placing and tracking orders, receiving deliveries, controlling stock and spares, and leading a simple ordering procedure. Good ordering keeps the job moving and the money under control.

blocks.p: On a small job, ordering is a list and a phone call. On a commercial job, it is a system: hundreds of items, several suppliers, long-lead equipment that must be ordered months ahead, and a programme that stops dead if one drum of cable is late. At Level 3 you build that system and lead the people who use it. This unit is for electricians who supervise jobs, run a contractor's store or look after a building's maintenance spares.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Take off quantities from the latest drawings, schedules and specification, add drops, tails and waste, and check the store before ordering.
Write each line with its part number, rating, size, material, standard and unit of measure, so that the supplier cannot send the wrong thing.
Work back from the date needed using the supplier's lead time, order long-lead and imported items early, and schedule deliveries to suit the site.
Raise requisitions, get approval within limits, send purchase orders, check confirmations and keep an order tracker.
Amend orders when the design changes, and get substitutes approved before they are ordered.
Chase late orders, get facts in writing, find alternatives and re-plan the work.
Check deliveries against the order, sign only for what arrived, record problems, claim in time and store safely.
Set minimum, reorder and maximum levels, count stock, record issues against jobs, and decide which maintenance spares to hold.
Write a simple procedure, train the people who use it, review supplier performance and keep the records.

ul: Jamaica's supply is **110/220 V at 50 Hz**. Much equipment on the market is made for 120 V or 230 V at 60 Hz or 50 Hz. Motors, pumps, fans, transformers and anything with a clock or timer must be checked for voltage **and** frequency before they are ordered.

Many electrical items are sold in **US units**: cable by the foot or in 500 ft rolls, conduit in 10 ft lengths, wire sizes in AWG. Metric cable (mm²) is also sold. The order must say which, and the take-off must be converted correctly.
Specialist items such as switchboards, generators and control panels are often **imported**. Allow for shipping, customs clearance and duty in both the lead time and the cost.
Prices are quoted with or without **GCT**. Compare like with like, and state which it is on every order.
Keep supplier prices and quotations confidential. Fair dealing with suppliers protects the firm's name and your own.

blocks.p: The sections follow an order from start to finish: working out what is needed, describing it, timing it, placing it, receiving it and storing it, then stock control and leading the system. Work the examples with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read every explanation, including the ones for questions you got right.

head: Document
What it gives you
rows: Positions and runs: outlets, switches, lights, containment routes, board positions. Check the revision box: an old drawing gives an old quantity.
The exact type and number of each fitting, the ways and breakers in each board, the size and length of each cable.
The standard each item must meet: cable types (for example LSZH in corridors), IP ratings, breaker types, makes where the designer has named one.
When each part of the work happens, so you know when each item is needed.
What the firm already holds, and whether it is free to use or set aside for another job.

blocks.note: The client's drawings and specification are part of the contract. An item that does not meet them can fail the inspection, be rejected by the client and have to be taken out at the firm's cost, however good the price was.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **take-off** turns drawings into quantities. The result is a **bill of materials (BOM)**: every item, its full description and its quantity, grouped so it can be ordered.

flow: Split the job into sections: containment, cables, wiring accessories, lighting, distribution and protection, special systems
Take off each section floor by floor, marking the drawing as you count
Measure cable and conduit runs to scale, then add vertical drops, rises and tails
Add a waste allowance
Convert to the supplier's units and round up
Write the full description for each line
Deduct usable stock
Have a second person check the totals

ul: A plan drawing shows runs across the ceiling or along the wall, but not the **drops** down to outlets and switches, the **rises** to lights, or the **tails** left for connection in boards and boxes. A take-off that misses them comes up short.

Example: a run of 18 m on plan feeds four outlets at 400 mm above the floor from a ceiling at 2.7 m. Each drop is about 2.3 m, and each end needs a 0.3 m tail: 18 + 4 × 2.3 + 5 × 0.3 = **28.7 m**, not 18 m.
A **waste allowance** covers off-cuts, small route changes and the lengths lost at the end of coils. About **5 to 10%** is common for cable; the firm's experience sets the figure.
Too little ordered stops the job; too much ties up money and ends up stolen, damaged or left over. The take-off is where the balance is set.

blocks.p: Suppliers sell in their own units: a 100 m coil, a 500 ft roll, a bundle of 10 lengths, a box of 25 glands, a pack of 100 ties. Convert the take-off to those units and **round up**.

head: Need
Unit of issue
Order
rows: 150 m of wire, priced by the foot

ul: Check the stock records **and** the shelves: records drift.
Deduct only stock that is **free**: not set aside for another job, not damaged, not out of date, and the same specification as the drawings ask for.
If a take-off calls for 14 breakers and the store's 5 are reserved for another job, the order is still for 14.

blocks.p: A supplier can only send what the order describes. 'Breakers, some, like last time' is a guess at both ends. Every line of an order carries enough detail that **two different people would pick the same item** from the shelf.

head: Item
Details the order must give
What goes wrong if one is missing
rows: Type (for example twin and earth, armoured, LSZH, THHN), conductor size (mm² or AWG), number of cores, conductor material, insulation and sheath, voltage rating, colour, length and whether in coils, drums or cut lengths
Aluminium arrives where copper was needed and the lugs and sizes are all wrong; PVC arrives where the spec asked for LSZH and it fails inspection

Number of ways, single or three phase, main switch or main breaker rating, busbar rating, breaking capacity (kA), surface or flush, IP rating, and each breaker's rating, poles and type, plus any GFCI or RCD
A board with breakers of too low a breaking capacity for the fault level cannot be used
Type, wattage and light output, voltage, colour temperature, beam angle, IP rating, mounting, emergency version or not, and the part number from the schedule
Indoor fittings arrive for an outdoor car park and fail when it rains
Power, voltage, **frequency (50 Hz)**, number of phases, speed, frame size, mounting and enclosure (IP) rating
A 60 Hz motor runs at the wrong speed and overheats
Part number, current rating, number of poles, breaking capacity, type (standard, GFCI, AFCI), and the board it fits
A breaker that fits the slot but is not listed for the board makes poor contact and overheats
Test voltages and functions, measurement category (CAT rating) and voltage, calibration certificate
An instrument with the wrong category is unsafe on a panel
Product, size, quantity, and that the safety data sheet (SDS) comes with it
Nobody knows how to store it or what to do in a spill

ul: Give the supplier's **part number** (catalogue number, product code) wherever you can. It is the shortest, surest description.
Give the **specification clause or schedule reference** too, so that the order can be checked back against the design.
Say what **standard** the item must meet where the specification names one.
For an item the supplier does not stock, mark it as a **special order** and expect a longer lead time and a deposit.
State the **unit of measure** (UOM) on every line: metre, foot, coil, length, box, each.

blocks.p: Cost of a line = quantity × unit price. Example: cable at J$210 per metre, three 100 m coils: 3 × 100 × 210 = **J$63,000** before GCT. Add GCT at the current rate only when you are told to, and say on the order whether prices include it. Check every total with a rough estimate: 300 m at about J$200 is about J$60,000, so J$63,000 is sensible; J$6,300 or J$630,000 is a slipped decimal point.

sections.title: Timing: lead times, scheduling and the order tracker

blocks.p: **Lead time** is the time between placing an order and the goods arriving. It covers the supplier's own stock or manufacture, shipping, customs and delivery. The **latest order date** is the date needed minus the lead time minus a safety margin.

blocks.note: **Example.** Special fittings have a lead time of 5 weeks and are needed on site on 24 July. With one week to spare, the latest order date is 24 July − 6 weeks = **12 June**. Mark it on the tracker and order before it, not on it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Item
Typical lead time
Why
rows: May need to be built up or ordered from the distributor
Main switchboards, generators, changeover switches, control panels
Made to order, shipped and cleared through customs

ul: Imported items need extra time for **shipping and customs**, and clearance can take longer than the shipping itself.
A supplier's quoted lead time is a promise about the future. Confirm it when you order, and chase before the date, not after it.
**Long-lead items** are ordered as soon as their design is approved, even if they are needed last. The main switchboard is often the first order and the last delivery.
**First-fix** items (containment, boxes, conduit, first cables) are needed early. **Second-fix** items (accessories, fittings, covers) are needed later.
Split a big bill of materials into **call-offs**: an order placed for the whole quantity at an agreed price, with deliveries called off floor by floor or week by week as the work reaches them.
A **blanket order** (framework or call-off contract) fixes prices with a supplier for a period, and items are drawn from it as needed. It saves raising a new order for every box of fittings.

head: Site
Delivery plan
rows: Downtown shop with no storage and a narrow street
Small deliveries booked to suit the work, taken straight to the point of use
Large hospital site with gates and security
Site address, gate number, delivery times and a named contact with a phone number on every order
New building with a secure store
Larger deliveries staged to the programme, so the store is never overfull

blocks.p: Staged deliveries also cut theft and damage, and keep money in the bank instead of on the site floor. Items with a **shelf life**, such as emergency lighting batteries, sealants and solvent cement, are ordered close to when they are needed.
An **order schedule** or **order tracker** is a shared spreadsheet or register with one row per order line or package. It is the tool that turns a pile of orders into a plan.

head: Column
Why
rows: Links the order to the design
Supplier, requisition number, purchase order number
Lead time; date needed; latest order date; date ordered
Promised delivery date; actual delivery date
Whether the supplier kept its word
Quantity received; shortage or damage; back-order

ul: Sort it by date needed and review it **every week** with the site supervisor.
Update it whenever an order is placed, confirmed, delivered or changed.
Raise any item at risk of being late at once, so the plan can change in time.
Keep it with the job file at the end; it explains costs and claims.

blocks.p: **Expediting** means chasing an order so that it arrives on time. It starts before the due date with a call to confirm, and it becomes urgent when the supplier warns of a delay.

flow: Get the facts in writing: the reason, the new date, whether part can come sooner
Tell the site supervisor and project manager at once
Check the programme for what depends on the item
Look for options: another approved supplier, an approved substitute, faster shipping, a temporary arrangement with the client
Re-plan so other work carries on
Tell the client about any effect on the finish date
Chase weekly; record every contact; note the supplier's performance

sections.title: Placing orders, approvals, changes and substitutes

flow: Requisition raised on site, with job number, full descriptions, quantities, units and date needed
Buyer checks it against the drawings, the specification and orders already placed
Buyer checks stock and gets prices from approved suppliers
Purchase order written with a unique number and approved within limits
Order sent; supplier's confirmation checked line by line
Order logged on the tracker and chased
Goods received and checked against the order and delivery note
Invoice matched to the order and the receipt before payment
Everything filed by job number

ul: A **requisition** is the site's request to the buyer. It is numbered, dated and signed, and it carries the job number so the cost lands on the right job.
One **requisition log** that everyone can see stops two people ordering the same thing.
An electrician does not phone the supplier from site, buy with his own money or take stock from another job's allocation. Those habits lose control of cost and of what is on the job.

A **purchase order (PO)** is the firm's written instruction to the supplier and the basis of the contract. It carries a unique number, the full description and quantity of each line, the agreed price, delivery address and date, the site contact, payment terms and whether GCT is included.
Most firms set **approval limits**: each person may approve orders up to a certain value, and larger orders go higher. The limits control spending and fraud.
An urgent order placed by phone is **confirmed in writing the same day** with the same order number, so that there is a record to check the delivery and invoice against.
An **online ordering system** linked to the stock records updates orders and stock together and removes copying errors, but every order still needs a person to check it.

blocks.p: The supplier's **order confirmation** (acknowledgement) is checked line by line against the purchase order: item, part number, rating, quantity, price and date. A confirmation that shows 16 A breakers where 20 A were ordered is queried at once and corrected in writing. Waiting for the wrong goods to arrive wastes everybody's time.

flow: Get the revised drawing or written instruction
Find every order the change affects
Not yet shipped: amend the order and get a revised confirmation
Already shipped: agree a return and any restocking charge, or use the items elsewhere
Record who agreed the change and what it cost

ul: When the specified item is out of stock and the supplier offers another make, get the **data sheet** and compare it with the specification: ratings, size, fixings, IP rating, certification, standard and warranty.
Order it only after the **designer or client approves it in writing**. The specification is part of the contract; a substitute may not fit, may not meet the design and may fail the inspection.
A delivery driver's opinion, or 'they are all the same', is not approval.
If a substitute is fitted without approval, the firm may have to take it out at its own cost.
Buy from the **approved supplier list**, and add a supplier only through the firm's process.
Do not show one supplier another's prices, and do not accept gifts or favours that could sway a decision.
Declare any personal connection with a supplier and step back from that decision.
Keep the records that show why each supplier was chosen.

sections.title: Receiving deliveries and dealing with problems

blocks.p: Have the **purchase order** ready, so you know what to expect and can check it. Plan where the goods will go and how heavy items will be moved: a cable drum needs a ramp or lift aid and more than one person.

head: Item
Check
rows: The delivery note matches the purchase order: item, part number, quantity, unit; the goods match the delivery note
Read the **sheath printing**: type, size, cores, voltage, standard. Check the drum or coil for damage, and the length marked on it
Rating plate, number of ways, breakers and their ratings, breaking capacity, door and busbars undamaged
Count the boxes, open a sample, check wattage, voltage, IP rating and the part number
Rating, poles, type and **batch number**, which goes on the receiving record so that a recall or fault can be traced
The SDS has come; the store is ready

ul: **Sign only for what actually arrived**, in the condition it arrived in.
Write any shortage, wrong item or damage on the delivery note **before** signing, and take photographs.
If you cannot check at once, sign 'unchecked' or 'received, not inspected', as the firm's procedure says, so that a later claim is not blocked.
The driver's hurry is not a reason to sign a clean note for a short or damaged delivery.

head: Problem
Action
rows: Sign for 18, note the shortage, record a **back-order** for 6 with its promised date, and tell the buyer
Wrong item (16 A breakers instead of 20 A)
Refuse that line or set it aside, note it, and ask the buyer to arrange the exchange
Note it, photograph it, keep it apart with a **quarantine label**, and claim at once; never use it or hide it
Do not sign for it; tell the buyer; return it as the supplier instructs
Unused items at the end of the job
Agree the supplier's **returns terms**, restocking charge and a **returns authorisation** before sending anything back

blocks.p: Check deliveries **when they arrive**, not weeks later. Suppliers accept claims for shortages and damage only within a set time, and a box opened a month later cannot prove when it was damaged.

ul: Enter the delivery on the **goods received record** and the order tracker: date, quantity, batch numbers, problems.
Update the bin cards or stock spreadsheet.
Report any problem to the buyer the same day.
The receiving record, the delivery note and the purchase order are what the **invoice** is checked against before it is paid: no payment for goods that did not arrive.

head: Item
Store it
rows: On their rims (flanges), on firm level ground, chocked so they cannot roll, cable ends sealed, under cover or out of strong sun
Flat, on shelves or pallets, dry
Dry, in their packaging, upright or as the maker says, away from dust, paint and building work until fitted
Boxed, on shelves, stacked no higher than the boxes can take
Cool and dry, and fitted soon: they lose charge and life in storage
In a ventilated, locked store away from heat and sparks, with the SDS to hand and a spill kit
On the floor or low shelves, moved with trolleys, drum stands or team lifts

blocks.p: Stock is money sitting on a shelf. Too little stops jobs; too much ties up cash, takes space, gets damaged, goes out of date and walks away. Stock control sets how much to hold and when to reorder, and keeps a record of where every item went.

head: Level
Meaning
rows: The amount kept back to cover a late delivery or a sudden job. The stock should rarely fall below it.
The point at which a new order is placed: **use during the lead time + safety stock**.
The most that should be held, so that money and space are not wasted.
Roughly the maximum less the stock that will be left when the new goods arrive.

blocks.note: **Example.** The store uses about 60 boxes of cable ties a month. Delivery takes 2 weeks (half a month), and the safety stock is 20 boxes. Use during the lead time = 30 boxes. Reorder level = 30 + 20 = **50 boxes**. The maximum is 120 boxes. When stock reaches 50, about 30 more will be used before the delivery arrives, leaving 20, so order 120 − 20 = **100 boxes**. If the lead time grows or use changes, the levels are reviewed.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A **bin card** or stock spreadsheet records every receipt and issue and the balance. Balance after an issue = balance before − quantity issued.
Every issue is recorded **against a job number**, so that each job's material cost is known and the final account can be checked.
**Count the high-value and fast-moving items often**, and everything at the stocktake. A difference between the count and the record is investigated and the record corrected, not ignored.
Issue the oldest stock first (first in, first out), especially for items with a shelf life.
Keep the store locked, with one person responsible for it.

blocks.p: A building's maintenance team does not order against drawings; it orders against **what might fail**. The question is which spares to hold.

head: Ask
Decide
rows: How critical is the equipment? What stops if it fails?
A spare pump motor for a hotel's water supply is a **critical spare**; a spare desk lamp is not.
How long does a replacement take to get?
Long-lead parts for critical equipment are held in stock; parts available the same day in town need not be.
The fault history shows which parts are worth holding.
What does it cost to hold?
Cheap, fast-wearing items (lamps, drivers, fuses, batteries) are held in small quantities with reorder levels.

ul: Start from the **asset register**: pumps, motors, air-conditioning units, boards, lighting, emergency lights, generator and changeover switch.
Label each spare with its part number and the equipment it fits, keep it in the locked store and record it.
When a spare is used, **log it and reorder it at once**.
Review the list each year and whenever equipment changes.
When a breaker fails at a clinic on a Saturday and no spare is held, the answer is the right part from an approved source, not any breaker that fits the slot.

blocks.p: A small contractor needs a procedure that fits on one page and that everyone follows.

ol: The site raises a **numbered requisition** with the job number, full description, part number, quantity, unit and date needed, after checking the store.
The buyer checks it against the drawings and specification and against orders already placed, and gets prices from approved suppliers.
A **purchase order** with a unique number, full descriptions, prices, delivery address, contact and dates is signed by someone allowed to approve that value.
The order is sent, the confirmation is checked, and the order goes on the **tracker**.
The order is chased as the date comes near.
The delivery is checked against the order and the note; problems are recorded and reported.
The invoice is matched to the order and the receiving record before payment.
Everything is filed by job number.

ul: When a store clerk keeps ordering the wrong type of breaker, the first step is to **check his orders before they go and train him on the specification**, not to take the job away or let the supplier choose.
Explain *why* each detail matters, with an example of what went wrong when it was missing.
Give people the documents they need: the specification, the schedules, the approved supplier list, the units-of-issue list.
Check a sample of orders and receipts each week.

head: Who tells whom
When
rows: Materials are being used faster than planned, so more can come before the work stops
Buyer tells the site and the project manager
A supplier warns of a delay, so the work plan can change in time
The design changes, so orders are amended before goods ship
A confirmation is wrong, a delivery is short or damaged, or a change is needed

ul: Record each supplier's on-time delivery, shortages, damage, errors and how quickly problems were put right.
Raise repeated problems with the supplier, in writing, with the evidence.
Review the approved list regularly. A supplier that is often late and short is reviewed and may be replaced, however familiar it is.

blocks.p: Keep copies of every requisition, order, confirmation, delivery note, receiving record and invoice in the **job file**. They are how the job's costs are checked, how claims for shortages and damage are made, how a recalled batch is traced, and how a dispute with a supplier or client is settled months later.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the documents a take-off is built from and why the latest revision matters.
I can take off cable runs with drops, rises, tails and a waste allowance.
I can convert quantities to units of issue and round up correctly, including feet and metres.
I can check the store and deduct only stock that is free to use.
I can write a full description for cable, boards, fittings, motors, breakers and instruments.
I can explain why voltage and frequency must be checked for equipment used in Jamaica.
I can cost a line and check it with a rough estimate.
I can work out the latest order date from the lead time and the date needed.
I can explain long-lead items, call-offs and blanket orders, and schedule deliveries to suit a site.
I can set up an order tracker and say what each column is for.
I can explain what expediting means and what to do when a supplier warns of a delay.
I can describe the ordering cycle from requisition to filing.
I can explain approval limits and why a phone order is confirmed in writing.
I can check an order confirmation and act on an error.
I can handle a design change and a substitute offered by a supplier.
I can receive a delivery, check it, sign correctly and record problems.
I can deal with a short, wrong, damaged or unordered delivery, and arrange a return.
I can store cable, boards, fittings, batteries and solvents correctly.
I can set and use minimum, reorder and maximum levels, and keep a bin card.
I can decide which maintenance spares to hold.
I can write a simple ordering procedure, train people on it and review supplier performance.

head: What
How
rows: Plan length + drops + tails, then + waste
Quantity × unit price; check with a rough estimate
Date needed − lead time − safety margin
Use during the lead time + safety stock
Maximum − stock left when the delivery arrives

terms: The highest value of order a person may approve.
The part of an order the supplier could not deliver and will send later.
The supplier's number for a production batch, recorded so that a fault or recall can be traced.
The full list of every item and quantity for a job, drawn from the drawings and specification.
An agreement with a supplier at fixed prices for a set period, from which items are drawn as needed.
A delivery taken against an order already placed, as the work reaches it.
A spare held because the plant would stop if that part failed.
The supplier's list of what was sent, signed on receipt.
Chasing an order so that it arrives on time.
The record of what was received, when, and in what condition.
The time between placing an order and the goods arriving.
A register of every order with its dates, status and problems.
The supplier's code for an item in its catalogue.
The firm's written, numbered instruction to a supplier to supply goods.
Keeping damaged, wrong or suspect goods apart and labelled so they are not used.
The stock level at which a new order is placed.
A numbered request from the site or workshop to the buyer for materials.
The supplier's agreement, with a number, that goods may be sent back.
Safety data sheet: the maker's information on the hazards, storage and handling of a product.
An item the supplier does not stock and must order in for one job.
A different item offered in place of the one specified; needs written approval.
Measuring and counting quantities from the drawings.
The unit a supplier sells an item in: metre, foot, coil, box, each.

c1.title: A primary school extension in Black River
c1.text: Ms Alicia Barrett, a Level 3 electrician, is preparing the bill of materials for a new classroom block at a primary school in Black River, St Elizabeth. The drawings are at revision C, but the copy in the site office is revision B. The specification asks for LSZH cable in the corridors. The lighting run on the plan is 46 m across the ceiling, with 8 drops of 2.4 m to switches and 10 tails of 0.3 m; the firm adds 10% for waste. Cable is sold in 100 m coils. The store holds 2 coils of the right cable, but one is reserved for another job.

c2.title: Pumps for a hotel in Runaway Bay
c2.text: Mr Devon Clarke, a Level 3 electrician, is ordering two replacement pool-circulation pumps for a hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann. A supplier's catalogue lists a pump at a good price, rated 230 V, 60 Hz, single phase. The hotel wants the pumps running before the winter tourist season begins on 15 December. The supplier quotes 7 weeks for the correctly rated pump, and the firm likes a week in hand. Devon's own cousin runs a small electrical supply shop in Ocho Rios.

c3.title: A late switchboard at a factory in Spanish Town
c3.text: Mrs Simone Hyatt is the buyer for a contractor fitting out a garment factory in Spanish Town, St Catherine. The main switchboard was ordered from overseas with a 12-week lead time. In week 9 the supplier emails that the board will be 5 weeks late, and in the same week the designer issues a revised drawing changing 40 of the 120 light fittings, which have already been ordered but have not shipped. A local supplier says he can offer a different make of switchboard from stock.

c4.title: A delivery at a hardware warehouse in May Pen
c4.text: Omar Francis, a Level 3 trainee acting as site storeman, receives a delivery at a new hardware warehouse in May Pen, Clarendon. The purchase order shows 30 LED high-bay fittings, 2 drums of 4-core 16 mm² armoured cable and 12 two-pole 30 A breakers. The truck brings 24 fittings, 2 drums whose sheath printing reads '4-core 10 mm²', and 12 breakers that are marked 30 A single-pole. The driver says he has three more drops to make and asks Omar to sign the delivery note so he can leave.

c5.title: The maintenance store at a Kingston office tower
c5.text: Ms Kerry-Ann Dixon has taken over the maintenance store of an office tower in New Kingston. The store uses about 80 LED lamps a month; the supplier delivers in 3 weeks (three-quarters of a month) and she keeps 30 lamps as safety stock. The maximum level is 200 lamps. The tower has two booster pumps for its water supply; a replacement motor takes 8 weeks to import, and one failed two years ago. The store also holds 9 boxes of a sealant that passed its use-by date last year, and the bin card for 20 A breakers shows 36 while the shelf count is 31.

questions.q: What should Alicia do before she starts the take-off?
o: Take off from revision B and adjust later
Get the revision C drawings and take off from those
Take off from both revisions and order the larger quantity
Ask the supplier to recommend quantities for a block this size
questions.why: A take-off from an old revision counts things that have moved or gone, and misses things that were added. Only the latest revision is used, and the revision is written on the bill of materials so that a later change can be traced.

questions.q: How many 100 m coils does the lighting run need altogether, before the store's stock is considered?
o: 2 coils
3 coils
4 coils
1 coil
questions.why: Length = 46 + 8 × 2.4 + 10 × 0.3 = 68.2 m. With 10% waste: 68.2 × 1.1 = 75 m, which is one 100 m coil (round up, never down). The store's free coil can then be issued against this job; the reserved one cannot. Taking off the 46 m on the plan alone would also give one coil here, but only by luck.

questions.q: The corridor cable order says only '2.5 mm² twin and earth, 300 m'. What is the problem?
o: Twin and earth is never sold by the metre, only by the coil
A quantity in metres cannot be converted into whole coils
The order must name a sheath colour before it can be sent
It does not say LSZH, so plain PVC may be sent
questions.why: The specification calls for LSZH in the corridors, and a supplier sent an order for '2.5 mm² twin and earth' will send its standard PVC cable. It would fail the inspection and have to be replaced at the firm's cost. Every line must carry the detail the specification demands.

questions.q: Alicia costs 4 coils of corridor cable at J$215 per metre. What is the cost before GCT?
questions.why: 4 coils × 100 m = 400 m, and 400 × J$215 = J$86,000. Check with a rough estimate: 400 m at about J$200 is about J$80,000. J$8,600 and J$860,000 are slipped decimal points, and J$43,000 is the cost of only two coils.

questions.q: What is wrong with the pump in the catalogue?
o: It is single phase, and pumps must be three phase
Its 60 Hz rating does not suit Jamaica's 50 Hz supply
230 V is far too high for any Jamaican supply
Nothing, as the supplier would set it to 50 Hz on delivery
questions.why: Jamaica's supply is 50 Hz. A motor made for 60 Hz runs at the wrong speed on 50 Hz and can overheat, and a pump would deliver less water. Voltage and frequency are both checked before any motor, pump or fan is ordered; suppliers do not 'set' the frequency.

questions.q: What is the latest date on which the correctly rated pumps should be ordered?
o: 20 October
27 October
3 November
10 November
questions.why: Work back from 15 December: 7 weeks' lead time is 27 October, and a week in hand gives 20 October. Order before that date, record it on the tracker and confirm the lead time with the supplier when the order goes in.

questions.q: Devon's cousin offers to supply the pumps a little cheaper than the approved suppliers. What should Devon do?
o: Order from his cousin, since the firm saves money
Order from his cousin, but ask him not to mention the connection
Declare the connection and step back from that decision
Refuse quietly and never tell anyone about the offer
questions.why: A buyer with a personal connection to a supplier cannot be seen to choose fairly, even if the price is good. The connection is declared, someone else decides, and the cousin's shop can only be used if it is added to the approved list through the firm's process.

questions.q: What should Simone do first about the late switchboard?
o: Cancel the order and accept the local supplier's board instead
Wait until the new date passes, then claim for the delay in writing
Get the new date in writing, and tell the site and project manager
Keep the news to herself until she has found a solution to offer
questions.why: The site must know at once, so the programme can be re-planned around the board. Getting the facts in writing, including whether part of the order can come sooner, gives everyone a sound basis for decisions. Options are looked at next, not before.

questions.q: The local supplier can offer a different make of switchboard from stock. What must happen before it is ordered?
o: The designer or client approves it in writing
The local supplier confirms in an email that it is the same thing
The site team agrees that it will fit the space on the wall
The overseas order is cancelled, so the firm is not charged twice
questions.why: The switchboard is a specified item and part of the contract. Its data sheet is compared with the specification, and only the designer or client can accept a different make. Fitting an unapproved substitute risks rejection at inspection and removal at the firm's cost.

questions.q: What should Simone do about the 40 light fittings that the revised drawing changes?
o: Let them arrive, store them and use them on a later job instead
Refuse the whole fittings delivery when the truck arrives on site
Ask the site to fit the old fittings and tell the client afterwards
Amend the order before the fittings ship, and get a new confirmation
questions.why: Because the fittings have not shipped, the order can be amended at little or no cost. The buyer sends the change in writing, gets a revised confirmation and records who approved the change. Once goods have shipped, returns and restocking charges come into play.

questions.q: Which item on the garment factory job should have been ordered first, and why?
o: The conduit and boxes, because first fix starts first
The cable, because it is the heaviest item to deliver
The switchboard, because its lead time is the longest
The light fittings, because there are the most of them
questions.why: Long-lead items are ordered as soon as their design is approved, whatever their place in the programme. The switchboard, made to order and imported, is usually the first order placed and the last to arrive. Quantity and weight do not decide the order date.

questions.q: What is the right way for Omar to deal with the 24 fittings?
o: Sign for 30 to let the driver go, and sort out the shortage later
Refuse all 24 until the full 30 can be delivered together on one truck
Sign for 24, note the shortage and record a back-order for 6
Sign for 24 and order 6 more fittings from another approved supplier
questions.why: He signs only for what arrived, writes the shortage on the delivery note and records a back-order with its promised date on the tracker. Refusing the 24 holds up the job; signing for 30 means the firm pays for goods it never received.

questions.q: What should Omar do about the two cable drums?
o: Accept them, since 10 mm² is close enough to 16 mm² for lighting
Accept them, as the drums can be used on another job in the future
Accept them, because the sheath printing is often wrong on drums
Reject them, note the error on the note and tell the buyer
questions.why: The sheath printing is the cable's identity, and 10 mm² will not carry the current designed for 16 mm². The wrong line is refused or set aside, written on the note before signing, photographed and reported, so that the buyer can arrange an exchange and the invoice is not paid for the wrong goods.

questions.q: Why must the 30 A single-pole breakers not be used in place of the two-pole breakers ordered?
o: A 220 V circuit needs both lines switched off together
Single-pole breakers are made only for ratings below 30 A
Single-pole breakers do not fit the busbar of any panel
Single-pole breakers cannot be fitted with a circuit label
questions.why: The two-pole breakers were ordered for 220 V circuits, which must open both lines at once. With two single-pole breakers, one could trip or be switched off while the other leaves the appliance live. The breakers are the wrong item and are treated as such on the delivery note.

questions.q: Omar records the batch number printed on each box of breakers. What is this for?
o: So the supplier can be paid for each batch separately
So the breakers do not need testing after installation
So the store can reuse the boxes for returns
So a faulty or recalled batch can be traced to the job
questions.why: If the maker later recalls a batch, or a breaker fails in service, the batch number on the receiving record shows which job and which panel the breakers from that batch went to. Without it, every breaker from that supplier would have to be checked.

questions.q: At what stock level should Kerry-Ann reorder the LED lamps?
o: 30 lamps
60 lamps
90 lamps
110 lamps
questions.why: Reorder level = use during the lead time + safety stock. Use during 3 weeks (three-quarters of a month) = 0.75 × 80 = 60 lamps. 60 + 30 = 90 lamps. Reordering at 30 would leave the store empty before the delivery arrived.

questions.q: When the lamps reach the reorder level, about how many should Kerry-Ann order to bring stock back to the maximum when the delivery arrives?
o: About 200 lamps
About 110 lamps
About 170 lamps
About 90 lamps
questions.why: About 60 lamps will be used while waiting for the delivery, leaving about 30. To reach the maximum of 200, order 200 − 30 = 170 lamps. Ordering 200 would take the store over its maximum and tie up money and space.

questions.q: Should the store hold a spare motor for the booster pumps?
o: Yes: the pumps are critical and the lead time is 8 weeks
No: a motor that failed only once in two years is reliable
No: the maintenance budget should go on items used every month
Yes, but only after the next motor has actually failed
questions.why: If a booster pump motor fails, the building's water supply is at risk, and a replacement takes 8 weeks to import. That makes it a critical spare, worth holding whatever its failure rate. Items that can be bought the same day in town need not be stocked.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do about the difference between the bin card (36) and the shelf count (31) for the 20 A breakers?
o: Investigate the difference, then correct the record
Change the bin card to 31 and say nothing further
Leave the bin card at 36, as the record is usually right
Order 5 breakers so the shelf matches the bin card
questions.why: A difference means that either an issue was not recorded or stock has gone missing. It is investigated first, so the cause is found, and then the record is corrected to the true count. Ordering to match a wrong record hides the problem.

questions.q: What does the 9 boxes of out-of-date sealant tell Kerry-Ann about how the store has been run?
o: Sealant was ordered in bulk for a job that was cancelled at short notice
Shelf-life items were ordered too far ahead and not rotated
The previous storekeeper always bought from the wrong supplier for sealant
The sealant was stored at the wrong temperature and spoiled early
questions.why: Items with a shelf life are ordered close to when they are needed, in sensible quantities, and issued oldest first. Nine boxes past their date mean money wasted and a product that may no longer cure properly. The levels for such items are set low.
